THE MINNEAPOLIS PLAN.
A Negro Ravisher in Ohio Hung by Indignant Citizens on the Spot Where His Terrible Crime Was Committed—Louisville Furnishes Another Victim.

CLEVELAND, Ohio, April 30.—A Galion dispatch says: The negro ravisher Fisher, was captured at five o'clock this morning at Frederickstown, Knox county, by two officers, just as he was leaving this place afoot. Fisher denied his name but was recognized, arrested and taken in a carriage to Galion, where he was put in an iron cage in the city prison about noon, arrangements being made to send him to a jail in some neighboring county to prevent threatened lynching, but at 3 o'clock a large crowd of determined people unmasked, went boldly up to the city hall prison and demanded the surrender of the negro to them. The officers refused and Mayor Underwood and others made speeches to the excited throng, counseling that the law be permitted to take its course, but to no purpose.

The mob forced the doors of the prison, broke down the iron cage and dragged the negro into the street with fierce shouts. Meanwhile a delegation accompanied by physicians who had been pressed into the service, drove to the house of the victim of the negro's lust to ascertain whether the girl, Barbara Rettie, was morally and physically able to confront and identify the prisoner. She told the physician she could as she had often seen him chopping wood near her home. This being reported to the crowd the negro was marched to her home, preceded by men carrying a rope, and surrounded by a howling rabble. When Barbara saw the cowering wretch, she exclaimed: "That is the man," and fainted.

The noose was then thrown over the negro's head and he was dragged to a tree at the rear of the lot. Somebody suggested the scene of the rape was the fittest place to strangle him. This was the view of all, and Fisher was taken to the spot, when he was told that his time had come to die. He protested his innocence to the last, but the blood still perceptible on his clothing was evidence of guilt, as well as the girl's statement, and he was quickly strung up, when the crowd quietly dispersed.

JUDGE LYNCH ACES.
JUDGE LYNCH ACTS.
The Black Brute Who Outraged a Child at Galion Hanged by the People.
GALION, O., May 1.—Last Friday as Barbara Rettig, a German girl, thirteen years of age, was returning home from a neighbor's house, she was assaulted by Frank Fisher, a burly negro, dragged into the woods, repeatedly and brutally outraged, and left in an insensible condition. When she returned to consciousness and dragged herself home and told her story, there was intense excitement, and searching parties were immediately organized to look for the black beast and capture him if possible. Yesterday morning a negro answering to the girl's description was arrested in Frederickstown, Knox county, and brought here and lodged in jail. Immediately a crowd began to gather, and ominous threats of lynching were heard. The fire bells were sounded, whistles blown, and the people began to gather around the jail. The officers in charge of the jail were unprepared for an assault, and tried to induce the mob to leave. The Mayor also addressed the mob, advising order and counseling them to let the law take its course. All pleadings were vain. A rush was made, the jail doors forced, the prisoner's cell broken into, and the hapless wretch dragged out, howling and begging for mercy. The people seemed frenzied with fury, and the prisoner was dragged along the street, kicked, choked, and pelted with stones at every step. The negro was taken to the home of the injured girl and taken into her presence as she lay suffering the most intense pain, and unable to move. She was asked if the prisoner was the man who misused her, and she said, without hesitation, that he was the man. There was other and conclusive evidence against him, and he was told that his time had come to die. He was taken from the house and followed by a howling mob of at least two thousand people, dragged to the woods where his foul crime was committed, and bidden to make his peace with God, for his time was short. The scene was horrible. Fisher, with distorted face, shrieked for mercy and protested his innocence. He was told he could have five minutes to pray, but all the more he writhled and twisted and asked for mercy. To the very last he delared his innocence. When the five minutes were expired the hands of the shrieking wretch were pinioned, a rope was placed around his neck and the other end thrown over the limb of a tree. There was a moment's pause, and a pitiful scream of the victim was stifled as the rope was pulled up and he swung writhing in mid air. The crowd stood by until the last convulsive struggles were over, and then disappeared, leaving the body hanging, and where it remained all night. There are but few people who condemn the deed, however lawless, and the general sentiment is that it was well done.

LYNCHED.
Frank Fisher Taken From the Gallon Jail and Hanged.

GALION, Ohio, April 30, 1882.

This has been the most exciting day in the history of the city and county. Frank Fisher, the negro who so horribly outraged the little German girl, Barbara Rettig, aged only thirteen years, in the woods, where he had been chopping wood last Friday noon, and who escaped, was captured about five o'clock this morning at Fredericktown, Knox County, by Officers T. J. Wurts and W. H. W. Nichols, of this city. The arrest was made just as the negro was about to leave Fredericktown on foot. He was first accosted by Officer Wurts, who asked him whether his name was Frank Fisher. "No, sah, that is not my name, sah," he replied, but Officer Nichols knew him, and after a few more questions, among which was asked why he had left Galion, he replied that he had got tired of chopping wood and thought he would skip. The officers, of course, arrested him, and at once started with him in a carriage, accompanied by two Fredericktown officers, for this city, arriving here at 11:30 this morning. The prisoner was at once taken to the jail in the City Hall and confined in one of the heavy iron cages, and the Mayor and city officers were laying plans to take him to the county jail at Bucyrus, or some other jail in some neighboring county, fearing that the loud threats of lynching would be carried out if Fisher would remain in the City Hall cell. Their fears were well founded, for the news of Fisher's capture spread through the city and the neighboring town like wild-fire, and at three o'clock this afternoon a large crowd of determined men boldly, defiantly and unmasked, with hammers, crowbars and other implements, and a huge and significant loop-rope, presented themselves before the entrance of the City Hall prison and demanded that Frank Fisher, the negro rapist, be surrendered into their hands. The officers of course refused. Then ensued a terrible scene of strife. The handful of officers were powerless, and the speeches of Mayor Underwood, G. M. Zeigler and others, who begged the excited crowd to let the law take its course and deal with the prisoner whose blood they sought, were unavailing and unheeded. With their implements of destruction they forced open the doors as though they were paper, broke open the iron cage that contained the guilty, trembling wretch, and grasping him with a dozen hands, as in a vise, they pulled him out into the street with a defiant shout. Previous to this, however, a delegation accompanied by a physician, whom they had pressed into service, drove furiously down to the residence of the victim of the negro's lust to ascertain whether she was in a proper mental and physical condition to see the negro for identification. The physician states to your correspondent that he asked her whether she knew the negro who had caused her misery. She replied yes, that she had often seen him while he was chopping wood near their home, and described his appearance. Being asked whether she could identify him, she replied she could. The delegation being satisfied reported at the City Hall, and then the scene that has been described was enacted. With hoots, yells and cheers, the crowd, preceded by some men and boys, bearing the fatal rope, marched with the frightened negro to the Rettig residence, at the foot of South Market Street, just south of the city limits, and took the black beast into the presence of Barbara Rettig, the little girl whom he had so horribly outraged. As soon as her eyes fell upon the cowardly and cowering wretch before her, she exclaimed: "That is the man who did it," and soon fainted with the terrible recollections.

The crowd threw the rope over the negro's head and dragged him to a tree in the rear of the lot, but some one suggested the woods—the scene of his terrible crime—hard by as the fit place to expiate his crime, and to the woods where he had been but a few pays ago chopping wood Frank Fisher was dragged and told that his time to die had come. He protested his innocence to the last, but the blood stains upon his clothing and the girl's evidence, coupled with numerous lies to the officers, was enough to condemn him in the minds of the infuriated and desperate crowd; and hang him they would, for a trial by law would only send him to the penitentiary and cheat the gallows of as black-hearted a demon as ever trod the earth. But they let him pray for a short time. He said in his prayer, "O Lord, take care of me. I know that I am going to die, but I have many friends." The balance of his appeal was drowned by the cries of the crowd to string him up. His hands were tied behind his back, his feet pinioned, a handkerchief placed over his face, a steady pull was given on the rope, the end made fast to a stump, and at 4:10 the soul of Frank Fisher, the negro rapist, was sent to answer for his crime before a higher court than that of Crawford County; and at this writing (9 p. m.) his body still dangles in mid-air. It is estimated that at least two thousand people, men, women and children, among whom was your correspondent, witnessed the execution by Judge Lynch. A large number of people from Bucyrus, Mt. Gilead, Crestline and other neighboring towns witnessed the ghastly spectacle. We should have stated that while the negro was being taken by the crowd a fire alarm sounded, and the lynchers thought it a ruse to get them to disperse; but the alarm was genuine, a frame house on South Market Street, on the line of march to the woods, having caught fire. The lynching of Frank Fisher, in broad daylight, upon Sunday, by unmasked men, was one of the boldest affairs that has ever transpired in this county. While the affair is to be regretted the crime was such that he has not a particle of sympathy from any one who has heard the particulars of the crime for which he has so dearly paid with his life. The Coroner of the county has been notified and may yet to-night hold an inquest and render a verdict. There is some talk of having the leading lynchers indicted by the grand jury, but it would not be safe to attempt that at present.

LITTLE ROCK, May 29. In the vicinity of Parker's store, 10 miles south of this place, there occurred last night a terrible tragedy, the victim being a negro boy named James Sanders, who on Saturday attempted to outrage Miss Nannie Carr, The young lady was sweeping out the church and school-house on the eve of the day named, when she heard a noise and looking up, saw Sanders before her and with a gun on his shoulder. A desperate struggle followed, the young girl fighting fiercely to preserve her honor. She screamed loudly, when Sanders seized her by the throat saying that he would kill her if she made another outcry. She gasped and struggled, pulling her assailant toward the door. About midnight the rude building was surrounded by a number of masked men, who overpowered the guards, broke down the door and riddled Sanders with bullets.

The Iron Mills Resume Work.
CINCINNATI, OHIO, June 12.—The iron mills in this city, Covington, Newport, and Aurora, are all under headway to-day, under the agreement made on Saturday.

The National Mercantile Travelers' association will begin its session here to-morrow. The chief object of the meeting is to create an influence in favor of legal measures to protect the rights of traveling salesmen in the south and west.

Lynched This Morning.
CHARLESTON, S. C., June 12.—The negro John Johnson, who outraged Miss McDowell, at Rock Hill, yesterday, was lynched this morning.

The New York Horse Shoers' Strike.
NEW YORK, June 12.—The horse shoers, who, on Saturday last, were commanded by the union to quit work, resumed it this morning in the Second and Tenth avenue car stables, matters having been arranged satisfactorily. No additional concessions were reported this morning, and both sides maintain their position with determination.

CHARLES BOOTH, aged 17, was drowned while bathing near Topeka, Kans., June 10.

MRS. MAGGIE LANGO, of Chicago, fell from a third-story window to the sidewalk, a distance of forty feet, June 10, striking on her head and shoulders, and she died on the way to the hospital.

AGILDIUS HOCK, a German, drew a razor from his pocket and cut his throat from ear to ear in St. Mary's Catholic Church, Buffalo, N. Y., June 11, and then rushed for the street, where he hacked himself again, and fell into the gutter and expired. The worshipers were transfixed with horror, women screamed and fainted, and great confusion prevailed.

THE Linn County Bank, at Brookfield, Mo., was entered on the afternoon of the 7th and robbed of nearly $5,000. Five men entered the bank, and while Cashier John Ford turned to make change presented drawn revolvers. The sixth man detained a lady at the front door while the robbery was going on. Cashier Ford and his sister-in-law were the only persons in the bank when the robbers entered. The thieves went out the back door, and left Brookfield in a northerly direction. Immediately after the robbery a posse of men, headed by the Marshal of Brookfield, gave hot pursuit, and after an exciting chase, during which shots were freely exchanged, the robbers were run into a log house, surrounded, and compelled to surrender. They gave their names as Winfield Allen, Frank Mason, Fred Mason, and Burt Ward.

THERE was a triple lynching at Lawrence, Kans., June 10. George Robertson, King, and Peter Vinagar, the negroes who murdered David Bausman, were taken from jail by masked men and hurried to the bridge, where ropes were placed about their necks and they were dropped off.

The envelope factory at Rockville, Conn., owned by White, Corbin & Co., was damaged by fire and water, June 10, to the extent of $100,000.

A powder magazine at Davenport, Iowa., was struck by lightning the other night. Stones were hurled in every direction, one weighing 80 pounds a quarter of a mile. A horse was killed at a distance by another stone. One was thrown into a house, striking a bed where two children slept. Windows were broken a mile away.

A boat containing four persons went over a dam on Fox River, June 11, and Mr. and Mrs. Priest, of Neenah, Wis., were drowned.

A boiler exploded at the Edgar Thompson steel works, Braddock, Pa., June 11. Assistant Superintendent Adair was fatally injured and three workmen were hurt.

Mrs. J. W. Barrett, of Washington, D. C., was killed on the steamer Star of the East, at Bath, Me., June 10, by a collision with a schooner. Several other passengers were seriously injured. The steamer was greatly damaged.

James Freeman, 23 years of age, of Acton, Mass., shot himself through the heart, June 11.

Mary Connors, residing in New York, has been placed in the Tombs on a charge of deliberately starving a small boy.

Two unknown tramps were cremated in a barn at Painesville, Ohio, June 10. The fire is attributed to careless smoking.

At Malden, England, the other day, Sir Claude de Crespigny made an ascension with an aeronaut named Simmonds, intending to cross the Channel. The car struck a house, and De Crespigny fell out and broke his leg. Simmonds was swept onward, and was seen over Calais in the afternoon.

JOHN JOHNSON, a negro who assaulted a little white girl, was taken from jail at Rock Hill, S. C., June 12, and hanged to a tree.

J. H. HARTMAN, aged 15, rushed out of his father's house, near Davenport, Iowa, the other night, and ended his career by plunging into the river. His mind had been affected for some time, presumably by bathing while too warm.

An obstinate cow threw a Baltimore & Ohio train from the track, near Martinsburg, W. Va., June 11, causing a general wreck. Several passengers and a newsboy were injured—none seriously.

PUGILISTS of Providence, named James Murray and Benjamin Green, went to Coney Island to contend for $300 and the light-weight championship of Rhode Island. Three rounds had been fought in a hotel when the metropolitan police captured Murray and his second, the others escaping.

The United States Commissioner at Buffalo, N. Y., held R. Porter Lee and Herman J. Hall for trial in the federal court at Canandaigua for embezzling the funds of the First National Bank. Lee's bail was fixed at $150,000, and he will lie in jail. Hall will be released on giving $10,000 security for his appearance.

CRIMES AND CRIMINALS.
A masked mob of 100 men burst the doors of the jail at Lawrence, Kan., secured Peter Vinegar, Isaac King and George Robertson, and hung them to the bridge timbers, for the recent murder of Daniel Bausman.

Lynching as a penalty for atrocious crimes is becoming a common occurrence in various parts of the country. Three cases of the kind occurred in one day last week. A negro in South Carolina guilty of outraging a white girl, a negro in Mississippi who had attempted the same crime upon a child, and a half-witted railroad laborer who had killed a fellow-workman at Las Vegas, N. M., were the victims.

At Lawrence, Kan., a public meeting of colored men denounced the lynching of the three negroes who murdered farmer Bausman. Tibbetts, the boy hanged for a double murder at Perham, Minn., is said to have been instigated to the crime by his own mother.

A dispatch from Las Vegas, N. M., says that "four rustlers, who bound and gagged Mason, a store-keeper, near Mesilla recently, robbing his store of all they could carry, were overtaken by a Mexican posse and strangled. All were Americans, but their names are unknown. They belonged to a gang of Arizona cowboys and richly deserved their fate."

In the jail at Geneva, Kane county, Ill., Deputy Sheriff Lawson killed James Irwin for a savage assault upon him and an attempt to release twenty prisoners. The officer was promptly vindicated by a Coroner's inquest.

The Brockfield bank robbers pleaded guilty, and received sentences of twenty-five years each in the Missouri Penitentiary. Their household effects were disposed of at auction at Kirksville, Mo., and brought enormous prices.

George McMillen, of Canton, Ohio, killed his wife with a revolver as she lay in bed, then fired a shot in his own shoulder and called the police, to whom he stated that a strange woman did the shooting.

—A negro named Mitchell was lynched at Mount Sterling, Ky., for a brutal outrage upon the wife of a respectable farmer.

—A Deputy Marshal captured at Carterville, Mo., three men who, for the past year, have been making spurious coin in a mining shaft. They had plaster-of-aria molds for manufacturing gold or silver coin of any denomination.

—At Jackson, Mich., a saloon-keeper named F. J. Schumacher fatally shot Policeman Schweimer, who had called to make his arrest; then mortally wounded his wife, who had taken refuge on a neighbor's porch, and then lay down on his bed and killed himself. The triple tragedy produced unusual excitement in the usually quiet town where it was enacted.

A black named John Johnson outraged Alice McDowell, aged 15, while she with other children were out hunting plums. He was caught, confessed, and was strung up. The Rock Hill men are not given to waste time fooling with court proceedings in such cases.

Denver, Col., June 17.—A special from Rico, Colorado says a party took out the murderers, Thomas Wall and Trinidad Charlie, and hung them in a small cabin opposite the jail. From the appearance of Charlie's body it is evident that he made a strong resistance. The men were shackled together by the leg and arm.

Albuquerque, N. M., June 17.—An Indian went to the ranche of Mr. Watkins at Dudley, and Mrs. Watkins being alone attempted to outrageously assault her, when she seized a Winchester rifle and shot him through the head.

At a dance at the house of John Mooney, in Indian Territory, on the night of the 10th inst., two young men named Montgomery and Horton got into a quarrel, which ended in both drawing pistols and shooting several times at each other. Montgomery was killed outright and Horton mortally wounded.

Two laborers named Monahan and MacAvoy quarreled at Steubenville, O., on the 11th inst. The latter was fatally stabbed.

At Linkville, Oregon, on the night of the 11th inst., a mob of masked men attempted to take a murderer named H. C. Lewis from the jail. Lewis fired on the mob, who responded with a volley, which killed the deputy sheriff and wounded Justice Wright. The would-be lynchers then retired.

A terrible tragedy was enacted at a school house at Harrisburg, Pernsett County, Ark., on the 7th inst. County Treasurer J. J. Smith remonstrated with the teacher for whipping his child. The conversation became heated and finally led to Smith's striking E. J. Wilmot, the teacher, on the head with a billet of wood, crushing his skull. The injured man died in three hours.

In a drunken quarrel at New Orleans on the night of the 7th inst., Richard Shea was stabbed to death by James Cosgrove.

An aged couple named O'Massey, living near Charlottesville, Va., were found murdered on the morning of the 8th inst., in their house. Money was the object.

A mob took Charles Shelton, John Redmond and Harry French from the jail at Los Lunas, Cal., on the 8th inst., and hung them to a tree.

A courtesan named Mary Sigman and her mother were assassinated at Mount Vernon, Ky., on the 8th inst.

A remarkable story comes from the City of Mexico. The report is that highwaymen attacked a stage full of armed men and that eleven of the outlaws were killed.

It is reported that nine Europeans journeying from Tunis to Gafsa were murdered between Tunis and Kairwan.

Advices from New Mexico are to the effect that Deputy Sheriff Miers and Martinez with a posse were attacked by Pueblo Indians while attempting to arrest some of the Pueblos who had escaped from jail. Miers was killed and Martinez mortally wounded.

A shocking tragedy took place at Boston, Mass., on the 7th inst. Mrs. Harriet Bell while returning from a grocery store near her home was accosted by an unknown man who followed her to the doorstep of her home and then cut her throat. She lived but a short time. The assassin escaped.

A brace of cattle thieves named Arnold Howard and Frank Young, in jail at Del Noter, Col., were visited by a mob on the 7th inst. Howard was killed outright and Young mortally wounded.

An affray with pistols took place at Arkansas City, on the 5th inst., in which J. W. Hale was killed by John Fuller.

Three negroes—Lewis Smith and Aaron and Ed. Clark—were killed in an affray at Arkadelphia, Ark., on the 6th inst. The shooting was done by Joe Ross and Thad. Henry, both white.

Tax Collector Robert Taylor was shot dead by Dr. Sims at Perryville, Perry County, Ark., on the 4th inst.

The Perry Home Journal says that at an early date there will be a chicken fight in Perry. All the cocks will be placed in the pit at once, and the owner of the last one to leave the pit takes all the other chickens as the prize of the victor.

The brick work on Seney Hall, at Oxford, is nearly complete; the slating has been put on three sides of the roof, and a good deal of the outside ornamental work finished. The work will go on rapidly now, and be complete by the first of July, at all events.

In Wild-cat di-trict, Forsyth county, last Sunday morning, William James shot a man just above the left nipple, the ball ranging downward and coming out under the shoulder blade.

Albany News and Advertiser: "The steam gin and grist mill of Mr. Sam. W. Livingston, of Newton, was destroyed by fire on Sunday night. The origin of the fire is supposed to have been incendary. The loss is estimated at $30,00. We are unable to state whether there was any insurance on the property or not."

Albany News and Advertiser: "Calvin, the old blind colored man, who pumps water at the Savannah, Florida and Western Railway tank in this city, met with a most unfortunate accident on Sunday. He fell between the depot platform and a box car and broke his leg in two places. He is in great pain, and it is hardly probable that he will ever be able to work any more."

Atlanta Post Appeal: "There is an important gathering of railroad magnates in the city at present, all of the lessees of the State Road being either here or represented. The object of this assemblage is a thorough discussion of the situation in view of the recent decision by Attorney General Anderson. A meeting was held Saturday and another will take place this evening. It is learned that no idea of abandoning the lease is entertained, and any effort to set it aside by the State authorities will be strenuously resisted."

Clayton, remembers distinctly when the Oconee river used to run down Broad street. This aged colored man says that he had a fish hole under the large sycamore trees where the National Bank now stands, and that he helped to ditch above Lincoln's plantation, and turn the river in its present channel. Thomaston correspondent Constitution: "Alice McCoy, colored, boarded the train en route to Barnesville from here, and when Conductor Hammond came around he found Alice in the ladies car, and tellin her to get out she refused. Mr. Hammond then ordered her taken out by the Marshal. Mr. Arnold Anderson, who happened to be at the depot. Thursday last suit was brought ag inst the Central Railroad by Alice, which resulted in the discharge of Conductor Hammond. Alice is the mother of Jesse and Whit, two boys who were sent to the chain gang from here last year for breaking in the store of Joseph Allen & Co., on Main street."

Chronicle and Constitutionalist: "Work on King Factory is progressing rapidly. Workmen are busily employed in all directions in breaking, leveling and hauling the ground where it will soon rear itself alongside the Sibley Mills. The foundation of the principal building will soon be completed. There are also in operation two brick molds. They both turn out about 50,000 brick daily. The clay is first wet and fed into the molds on one side as mud and comes out on the other side made into the form of bricks. They are then piled in rows, and after having been thoroughly dried by the sun, are put in the kins and subjected to a great heat for about five days, and then allowed to cool, and are afterwards taken out ready for being used to form the walls of the factory."

Atlanta Post-Appeal: "W. S. Wilson & Bro., coal and lumber dealers on Spring street, exhibited a shattered safe to a reporter this morning which showed the skill of an artist in safe burglary. A hole was drilled near the combination, filled with powder, the fastening blown asunder and the contents of the safe left to the mercy of the depreyders. They riffed the drawers and took the little iron box from its fastening, and going out to the lumber yard tipped it open with a chisel and scooped in its contents, leaving the box and a small drawer contained in it on a lumber pile. The Messrs Wilson are somewhat reticent as to the amount contained in the box, but state that there were fifty dollars in the drawer and a number of checks, which latter were left. The box may have contained one hundred or five hundred dollars. An entrance to the office was effected through the door, which offered little resistance. No cue was left as to who the thief or thieves were. It would be well, while these safe burglars are sojourning with us, for those who have no burglar proof safe to deposit their valuables in a vault for safety."

Monroe Advertiser: "The store of Mr. R. M. Williams, at iceberg, was entered and robbed last Thursday night. The store is set upon a rock foundation. This was broken through and the burglaries thereby got into the cellar and had no difficulty in entering the store therefrom. A large quantity of goods was stolen—value of which cannot well be calculated. Several of the negro workmen on the railroad were arrested on suspicion Friday, and tried before a magistrate, but the proof was not strong enough to warrant their commitment. None of the goods have been found. On Saturday a white man, named A. S. Averitt, was arrested in Macon, as the burglar. He had sold of the stolen goods, and thus he was traced. Mr. Williams being notified of his arrest, sent Mr. Little to Macon after him. He confessed the crime to Mr. Little, and had already confessed to the policeman who arrested him. He was brought to Forsyth and is now in jail. He seems to be a respectable man, and expresses deep regret for his crime, says it is his first offense and shall be his last. He is from Futnam county, and was at work on the railroad, previous to his crime."

Augusta News, 11th: "A young boy was saved from drowning in the canal this morning through the timely arrival and heroic exertions of a gentleman passing near the scene on McKinne street, over the third level of the canal. The little fellow, John Hardman, who lives in that neighborhood, fell into the water while playing with some companions, about a hundred yards from McKinne street. Their exertions to rescue him as he floated down the stream, which is swift at that place, were confined to holding out sticks to him, and while grasping at them he was several times carried under the water. While drifting helplessly along and when about to fail in strength he was seen by Dr. Frank M. Deems, Mr. George Howard and one or two others passing along the street. The two gentlemen named jumped from their vehicles, rushed down the bank, and Dr. Deems, who was first at the water, called to Mr. Howard to stay on the bank and not to jump in unless necessary. THE FIRE DEPARTMENT. Chief Engineer Galligan Turns Over the Keys to His Successor.
Chief Engineer J. J. Galligan, who for seven years conducted the affairs of the fire department of this city, once for a term of three years and again for four and a half, yesterday surrendered his office, keys and mantle of authority to Capt. John H. Butler, who was nominated by the mayor and confirmed by the council Tuesday night as chief.

The appointment was in many respects unsatisfactory to the boys, it being admitted that the election of April 13th, which saw Mr. Edward Welsh chosen to the office, was a legal one, and the protest made being decidedly mild. Capt. Butler may be a number one man, and prove a good chief, but he will have hard work to fill the place Jack Galligan has occupied for so long. There probably never was a better fireman in Omaha; he was always on time, foremost in fighting the fire and ready to brave any danger however great. He never asked a man to go where he wouldn't go, and many a time has gone where others dared not. After the catastrophe of September 5th 1878, when the city got a serious lesson on the subject of appointing men whose skill was to be tested and was not already proven, it would seem that that would have been enough and it was asserted yesterday by firemen and others that the first emergency will see another transfer of the office like the one in 1878.

The boys of No. 2 are indignant at the rejection of their candidate, Mr. Welsh, and called a meeting for yesterday at which there was a prospect of a lively time. Some are for disbanding and retiring from the service, and it may be that the business will end in the total disorganization of the department. Certainly the effort to harmonize the two factions in the department is by no means successful and harmony seems farther off than ever. It is said that the mayor merely wishes to keep up his reputation for doing what nobody else would think of doing.

THE FIREMEN'S MEETING.

At 8 o'clock last evening there was quite a large gathering at Firemen's Hall, and the meeting was called to order by the president of No. 2, F. J. McShane, who stated the object of the meeting.

It appears that a company meeting was held in the morning, at which steps were taken to ascertain the amount of funds in the company treasury, and also in the department treasury, the idea being to pay Mr. Edward Welch the amount in which he was the loser in the campaign for the position of chief engineer of the department.

It was, in accordance with the determination of this meeting, moved, that the secretary be instructed to draw a warrant for $50 on the treasurer, to be paid over to Mr. Welch, and this motion was carried.

Messrs. O'Byrne, Ryan and Ed Kosters were appointed a committee to hand

handsome secretary's desk to the now in progress at Creighton hall, this representing their part of the furniture in Firemen's Hall. The motion carried, and Messrs. Ed Kosters, Morris Hengen and Barney Shannon were appointed a committee to deliver the desk to the officers of the fair, and they did so on the adjournment of the meeting.

On motion the president was requested to appoint a committee of five to request the president of the department to call a general meeting as soon as possible, and the following were appointed as such committee: Barney Shannon, Jas. Teahon, I. W. Miner, Fred Lowe and Theo. Grebe.

WESTERN MOBS.—More than one dozen men have been hanged by mobs.
Western Mobs.—More than one dozen men have been hanged by mobs at the North and West during the past month. The average is one every other day. Our latest report is, O. W. Garrett taken from jail and hanged in the yard at Greensburg, Indiana, by 50 masked men. The victims had helped a negro to murder a white man.

At Minneapolis, a Boston scallawag named Tim Crawley, who had served a term in prison for outraging a couple of negro girls, coaxed the 4 year old daughter of Jason Spear, a prominent citizen, into the bushes, and left her in such condition that she has since died. Sixty men broke open the jail, and seized the wretch who showed not a particle of fear. He was marched to the house of Mr. Spear and fully identified the agonized mother exclaiming: "It is the man; take him away." While this scene was going on the victim of the villain lay dying in an adjoining room. He was placed under an oak tree, and a noose was prepared. While this was being done he was asked if he had anything to say. He said that he had a mother named Nancy Ann Crawley, living in South Boston. He then took a member of the vigilance committee aside and had a few moments private conversation, reposing in him something to be delivered to his mother at some future time.

The nerve of the wretch remained unshaken. When asked how he came to perpetrate the crime he said it was done while he was drunk."

St. Joseph, April 18—Intelligence was received here to-night of a horrible affair at Barnard, thirty miles from here. A tramp murdered a man named Alkire last night in cold blood. The citizens turned out and ran the tramp to cover, and found him entrenched securely in a lot of cord wood, where he could not be got at. They finally determined to blaze him out. Bottles filled with petroleum were pitched against the barricade, followed by lighted cotton. The heat ultimately forced the tramp out, and on his appearance was riddled with bullets, fifteen holes being found in him. No papers, letters or anything leading to his indentification were found. It is thought he was insane.
